items.sentence_raw: The discovery that language can be a barrier to communication is quickly made by all who travel, study, govern or sell.
items.explain: Q26: The question asks for a suitable title. The whole passage talks about problems with language as a barrier and how people try to solve them — **'Overcoming'** means beating or solving a problem. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Whether the activity is tourism, research, government, policing, business, or data dissemination, the lack of a common language can severely impede progress or can halt it altogether.
'Common language' here usually means a foreign language, but the same point applies in principle to any encounter with unfamiliar dialects or styles within a single language.
items.explain: Q18: The question asks what *'They don't talk the same language'* can refer to. The passage says *'the same point applies... to any encounter with unfamiliar dialects or styles within a single language'* — **'dialects or styles'** are different ways of speaking the same language. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: "They don't talk the same language" has a major metaphorical meaning alongside its literal one.
Although communication problems of this kind must happen thousands of times each day, very few become public knowledge.
Publicity comes only when a failure to communicate has major consequences, such as strikes, lost orders, legal problems, or fatal accidents - even, at times, war.
items.explain: Q14: The question asks when language problems get public attention. The passage says *'Publicity comes only when a failure to communicate has major consequences'* — **'publicity'** means public attention, and **'major consequences'** are big results like fatal accidents. So the answer is **major consequences**.

items.sentence_raw: One reported instance of communication failure took place in 1970, when several Americans ate a species of poisonous mushroom.
No remedy was known, and two of the people died within days.
A radio report of the case was heard by a chemist who knew of a treatment that had been successfully used in 1959 and published in 1963.
Why had the American doctors not heard of it seven years later?
Presumably because the report of the treatment had been published only in journals written in European languages other than English.
items.explain: Q19: The question asks what the mushroom case suggests about American doctors. The passage says *'the report of the treatment had been published only in journals written in European languages other than English'* — this means they only read articles in English. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Several comparable cases have been reported.

But isolated examples do not give an impression of the size of the problem - something that can come only from studies of the use or avoidance of foreign-language materials and contacts in different communicative situations.

In the English-speaking scientific world, for example, surveys of books and documents consulted in libraries and other information agencies have shown that very little foreign-language material is ever consulted.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks how we know the size of the language barrier. The passage says *'surveys of books and documents consulted in libraries... have shown that very little foreign-language material is ever consulted'* — **'surveys'** are studies that give evidence of the extent. So the answer is **surveys**.

items.sentence_raw: Library requests in the field of science and technology showed that only 13 per cent were for foreign language periodicals.
Studies of the sources cited in publications lead to a similar conclusion: the use of foreign-language sources is often found to be as low as 10 per cent.
The language barrier presents itself in stark form to firms who wish to market their products in other countries.

British industry, in particular, has in recent decades often been criticised for its linguistic insularity - for its assumption that foreign buyers will be happy to communicate in English, and that awareness of other languages is not therefore a priority.

In the 1960s, over two-thirds of British firms dealing with non-English-speaking customers were using English for outgoing correspondence; many had their sales literature only in English; and as many as 40 per cent employed no-one able to communicate in the customers' languages.
items.explain: Q16: The question asks for an example of British linguistic insularity. The passage says *'many had their sales literature only in English'* — **'sales literature'** means materials like brochures used for selling. So the answer is **sales literature**.

items.sentence_raw: A similar problem was identified in other English-speaking countries, notably the USA, Australia and New Zealand.
And non-English-speaking countries were by no means exempt - although the widespread use of English as an alternative language made them less open to the charge of insularity.
The criticism and publicity given to this problem since the 1960s seems to have greatly improved the situation.
items.explain: Q20: The question asks about the linguistic insularity of British businesses now. The passage says *'The criticism and publicity given to this problem since the 1960s seems to have greatly improved the situation'* — **'improved'** means it is not as bad now. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: industrial training schemes have promoted an increase in linguistic and cultural awareness.
items.explain: Q21: The question asks for one way British companies solved the language barrier. The passage says *'industrial training schemes have promoted an increase in linguistic and cultural awareness'* — **'training schemes'** are programs to teach skills. So the answer is **industrial training schemes**.

items.sentence_raw: Many firms now have their own translation services; to take just one example in Britain, Rowntree Mackintosh now publish their documents in six languages (English, French, German, Dutch, Italian and Xhosa).
items.explain: Q22: The question asks for another way British companies solved the problem. The passage says *'Many firms now have their own translation services'* — **'translation services'** help change words from one language to another. So the answer is **translation services**.

items.sentence_raw: Some firms run part-time language courses in the languages of the countries with which they are most involved, some produce their own technical glossaries, to ensure consistency when material is being translated.
items.explain:
Q23: The question asks for a third way British companies solved the problem. The passage says *'Some firms run part-time language courses'* — **'language courses'** are classes to learn a language. So the answer is **part-time language courses**.

Q24: The question asks for a fourth way British companies solved the problem. The passage says *'some produce their own technical glossaries'* — **'technical glossaries'** are lists of special words with meanings. So the answer is **technical glossaries**.

items.sentence_raw: It is now much more readily appreciated that marketing efforts can be delayed, damaged, or disrupted by a failure to take account of the linguistic needs of the customer.

The changes in awareness have been most marked in English-speaking countries, where the realisation has gradually dawned that by no means everyone in the world knows English well enough to negotiate in it.

This is especially a problem when English is not an official language of public administration, as in most parts of the Far East, Russia, Eastern Europe, the Arab world, Latin America and French-speaking Africa.
items.explain: Q17: The question asks where people may have difficulty negotiating in English. The passage says *'English is not an official language... in most parts of the Far East, Russia, Eastern Europe, the Arab world, Latin America and French-speaking Africa'* — any of these places is correct. So the answer is **the Far East** (or any other listed region).

items.sentence_raw: Even in cases where foreign customers can speak English quite well, it is often forgotten that they may not be able to understand it to the required level - bearing in mind the regional and social variation which permeates speech and which can cause major problems of listening comprehension.
items.explain: Q25: The question asks what English-speaking people need to be aware of. The passage says *'foreign customers can speak English quite well... they may not be able to understand it to the required level'* — this means even English-speaking foreigners may have difficulty. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: In securing understanding, how 'we' speak to 'them' is just as important, it appears, as how 'they' speak to 'us'.
